titleFa: کتاب The House of the Dead
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
introFa: کتاب «The House of the Dead» نوشته Fyodor Dostoevsky یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The House of the Dead»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

Daniel Beer, The House of the Dead: Siberian Exile Under the Tsars, Allen Lane: London, 2016; 455 pp.; 9781856145377, £30.00 (hbk) Sarah Badcock, A Prison Without Walls? Eastern Siberian Exile in the Last Years of Tsarism, Oxford University Press: Oxford, 2016; 191 pp.; 9780199641550, £60.00 (hbk) Reviewed by: Janet Hartley, London School of Economics and Political Science, UK Siberia was used as place of punishment and exile from the very beginning of the Russian over-lordship from the 1580s. By the 1660s, there were over 7000 exiles in Siberia and some 28,000 men and women were exiled in the period from 1662 to 1709. The most notorious exile in the seventeenth century was Archpriest Avvakum, who was exiled for his refusal to accept the changes to the liturgy and rituals of the Orthodox Church in the reign of Alexis, and who wrote the ﬁrst account of exile and of the cruel punishments inﬂicted upon him. Siberia has until the present day been associated in popular imagination, in Russia and abroad, with exile, punishment and suﬀering. In the House of the Dead: Siberian Exile under the Tsars, Daniel Beer describes the mechanism and experience of exile in Siberia in the nineteenth century and the beginning of the twentieth century. It is a good story and he tells it very well, enhanced by extensive but judicious use of archive materials, primarily from the records of ministries and the police department in St Petersburg and from local records in Irkutsk (although it would have been very helpful to have had some identiﬁcation of the sources he has used other than just the archive number). After a clear introductory overview of the exile system he concentrates on the experiences of several main groups of exiles: the mainly noble Decembrists exiled after an unsuccessful coup attempt in 1825; the Polish exiles after the revolts of 1830 and 1863; the Sakhalin communities in the second half of the nineteenth century; poli- tical exiles from the mid-nineteenth century, of which the most famous was Fedor Dostoevsky, through to the end of the tsarist period. His chronological coverage is interspersed with thematic chapters on the journey to Siberia, escaped convicts and their impact on local communities, punishments inﬂicted on convicts and changing perceptions within Russia on the exile system in the last decade of the nineteenth century. Beer has made excellent use of contemporary accounts of those who witnessed or experienced exile to give a vivid account of the sheer cruelty of the exile system. The suﬀering started with the journey itself, when, before the opening Book Reviews 531

of the Trans-Siberian railway, it often took years for the poor wretches to reach their place of incarceration or exile on foot, with heavy shackles, and very little provision made on the way for their shelter, sustenance or physical care. Particularly harsh conditions were experienced by those sentenced to hard labour in the Nerchinsk mines (including Decembrist exiles, amongst others), but also challenging was the struggle for survival in the extreme climate of remote settlements, including the Sakhalin peninsula. All exiles could be subjected to cruel and excessive punishments, often for minor infringements of the rules or simply arbitrarily. The story of human suﬀering is made more poignant by the many stories of often obscure individuals throughout the text. Beer also shows the impact of the exile system on local communities. The contact was, inevitably, often conﬂictive, as large numbers of escaped and desperate convicts roamed the countryside, but could on occasion be beneﬁcial as educated exiles attempted to set up schools and cultural facilities. The story of exile can become a relentless account of hardship and suﬀering, and, within that context, Beer could have made clearer distinctions between the those exiled for criminal activities (often with hard labour in the mines), and those exiled for perceived disreputable behaviour or religious beliefs in order to become village settlers in Siberia with the aim of encouraging agriculture. The attitudes towards the exile system by the central and local authorities did not, however, remain static. Beer shows that the attitudes of the local authorities in Siberia changed from the 1860s onwards and they became more wary as they had to deal with more ‘politicals’ who were willing to protest about their treatment and were able to publicize their experiences. By the 1890s, a public debate about the exile system was taking place in Russia, driven not only by more public awareness of the experiences of exile but also by the negative perception of exile in Siberia in the foreign press which was damaging Russia’s image. The weaknesses of the exile system which had been exposed by the end of the nineteenth century are richly illustrated by Sarah Badcock’s more specialized study: A Prison Without Walls? Eastern Siberian Exile in the Last Years of Tsarism. This excellent book complements Beer’s analysis by looking in detail at the experience of exile between the years 1905 and 1917 in one, particularly hostile, region of Eastern Siberia. It draws heavily on archival material from, in particular, archives in Yakutsk and Irkutsk. These unique sources enable Badcock not only to describe some of the same experiences as the nineteenth-century exiles – the hard labour (scarcely mechanized in the early twentieth century and still physically very demanding: death rates amongst those sentenced to hard labour were always extre- mely high), the journey (still very onerous, albeit now in part by train), the punish- ments (less common, and less barbaric, but still prevalent and traumatic) – but also to try to penetrate the day-to-day experiences and feelings of the exiles. Badcock mostly concentrates on the experiences of the ‘politicals’ in exile, rather than the criminals, because most of the contemporary materials are written about or by the former. By the early twentieth century the local authorities displayed almost a total inability to cope with the exiles and, far from being able to carry out 532 European History Quarterly 47(3)

proper surveillance of their activities, simply neglected and abandoned them in a hostile environment. The state, in Badcock’s words, was now ‘a shaggy and shabby beast’ (4), its ineﬃciency ruthlessly exposed by the press in Russia and abroad. In Siberia itself, at least if this region in eastern Siberia is typical, the so-called ‘system’ had almost completely broken down. Badcock describes exiles wandering from place to place, without any permission or escort, trying desperately to ﬁnd some work as they had been arbitrarily sent to various locations with no consideration of what they would do when they arrived. According to the records she found, 31,043 out of 72,136 exiles, comprising 43 per cent, sent to the Irkutsk region by 1913 had escaped (at least the prison inspectorate in Irkutsk kept these precise records!), although ‘escape’ might mean simply looking for work somewhere else rather than trying to get home. The impression given is of a chaotic situation in which exiles of all types simply tried to survive in the face of almost total indiﬀerence by the authorities to their fate. What Badcock is able to show is how the exiles lived on a day-to-day basis within this chaotic world. The majority of the exiles were men, but women and children were also caught up in the exile system, either as exiles themselves or as the partners and families of male exiles. Women also had to ﬁnd some means to survive and children, the innocent victims, sometime ended up abandoned in orphanages. Exiles came into contact with the non-Russian ethnic groups in eastern Siberia, in this case mainly Yakuts. The description of the day-to-day interaction of the exiles with the Yakuts, many of whom spoke no Russian, and, to an extent, their depen- dence on them, is one of the most fascinating insights of this book. The neglect of exiles extended beyond housing and occupation. Medical provision was almost non-existent and severe illness was common, especially tuberculosis and respiratory and gastrointestinal disease, and the death rate amongst exiles, particularly those who were held in prisons rather than those who were settled in villages, was shockingly high. The climate in eastern Siberia was extreme in temperature and humidity, but many exiles arrived already in a weakened condition after their journey from European Russia and were often in no condition to undertake the often physically demanding work expected of them. The detailed description of life in exile in eastern Siberia is itself an achievement, but Badcock also tries to penetrate the mind-set of the exiles, with considerable success. She shows how, even in the most extreme circumstances, such as the journey to Siberia or in simply trying to survive, friendships were formed amongst exiles. The shortage of ethnic Russian women amongst the exiles led, inevitably, to relationships forming and marriage between Russian exiles and Yakut women. The Russian state, attempting to follow the traditional tsarist policy, from at least the eighteenth century, of using exiles to settle Siberian villages, bizarrely still paid 50 roubles per household to encourage exiles to marry and establish themselves. There are also contemporary accounts of the kindness shown by the indigenous population towards the often helpless exiles, some perhaps exaggerated to contrast indigenous people with the unsympathetic local Russian oﬃcials, but others probably genuine. Finally, Badcock engages with the diﬃcult assessment of Book Reviews 533

the mental state of the exiles. We know that suicide rates were higher amongst exiles in Siberia than amongst the settled population or in European Russia in the nineteenth century. Contemporary memoirs and accounts strongly suggest that depression and anxiety were common amongst exiles in the region studied here. Statistics on suicides in the early twentieth century can be misleading, but the circumstances in eastern Siberia, particularly the sense of isolation and alcohol abuse, and the experience of exile in general, as well as the inﬂiction or prospect of corporal punishment, could lead to suicide, as in the tragic cases described by Badcock here. These two books are a signiﬁcant scholarly contribution to our understanding of the tsarist exile system in the nineteenth and early twentieth century. They both illustrate key features of the exile system: the complexity of the diﬀerent types of exiles in Siberia; the inability of the tsarist regime and the local authorities to manage the exile system; and the mostly negative eﬀect which exile had on the local communities in Siberia and, more broadly, on Siberia’s economic develop- ment. Above all these books are a sobering reminder of the cruelty inﬂicted by the state and by individuals on men, women and children and a testimony to human endurance in the face of this suﬀering. Jeff Bowersox, Raising Germans in the Age of Empire: Youth and Colonial Culture, 1871–1914, Oxford University Press: Oxford, 2013; 256 pp.; 9780199641093, £66.00 (hbk) Reviewed by: David Hamlin, Fordham University, New York, USA Raising Germans in the Age of Empire explores ways in which colonial assumptions were introduced to German children during the Kaiserreich. JeﬀBowersox presents an elegant treatment of the normalization of empire and racial hierarchy. Bowersox is principally interested in the construction of what he terms a ‘colonial archive’. Some attention needs to be paid to both of these terms. ‘Archive’ is used here rather as Paul Saint-Amour does in Tense Future – as the sum collection of images and ideas available to a society. Raising Germans, then, focuses on the construction of a discursive and imagined colonial world available to Germans who remained in the metropole. ‘Colonial’, meanwhile, refers not simply or even primarily to German colonial dependencies. Rather, Bowersox uses ‘colonial’ to reference the other side of a civilizational divide. Germans saw themselves, Europeans, and whites more generally, as bearers of modern, progressive civilization. ‘Colonial’ describes the Others, those in one fashion or another bereft of the ordering and pacifying power of western civi- lization. In eﬀect, ‘colonial’ referenced unruly, lightly or ungoverned societies in which individuals were both more free and more endangered. It functions as the geographically displaced Other to the increasingly interconnected and disciplined society of the industrial West.
